title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text: Course Cover

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Course Overview
Virtual and augmented reality, also known as immersive reality, is any technology that replicates an environment, real or imagined, and simulates a user’s physical presence and environment to allow for user interaction. Spatial computing enables immersive interaction by understanding the physical world, knowing and communicating our relation to places in that world, and navigating through those places.

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Who This Is For
This module is 100% continuously accessed. There is no terminal exam. Students must demonstrate understanding of the theoretical aspects of the subject through written assessment and learning journals / blogs that demonstrate understanding and reflecion in their research, design and development. Students’ practical design and development skills will be assessed by multi-faceted projects that require students to design, build, deploy and test a subject specific exemplar projects (e.g. VR/AR/XR Application or Game, motion tracking prototype, research & present on specified topic, etc )

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Demonstrate a critical understanding of the concepts and principles of 3D systems and augmented and virtual reality in the context of spatial computing
Explore, critique and deconstruct modern VR, AR, and spatial computing experiences.
Demonstrate theoretical understanding of, and practical competence in the use of advanced input and output devices & sensors in an immersive environment.
Apply appropriate principles of human-computer interaction to the construction and evaluation of virtual and augmented reality and spatial computing systems.

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
section: What is interaction design in XR?
text:
What is interaction design in XR?
Interaction design is the practice of designing how users act within a system.
In XR this includes:

how users select objects
how users move through space
how users manipulate digital content
how the system provides feedback

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Why XR is different
Traditional interfaces usually assume:

2D screens
mouse, keyboard, or touch input
a fixed viewpoint

XR systems introduce:

3D space
body-based interaction
dynamic viewpoint
spatial audio, haptics, and embodied feedback

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
The interaction loop





flowchart LR
  A[User intent] --> B[Input action]
  B --> C[System response]
  C --> D[Sensory feedback]
  D --> A
  






If any part of this loop is weak, the experience feels awkward, confusing, or uncomfortable.

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Core interaction questions
When analysing an XR experience, ask:

What is the main input method?
How does the user select or manipulate things?
What feedback does the system provide?
How does the user move?
What makes the interaction intuitive or frustrating?

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
UI paradigms

Diegetic UI
UI that exists within the world.
Examples: - a wrist display - a control panel on a wall - buttons attached to equipment


Non-diegetic UI
UI that exists outside the world fiction.
Examples: - HUD overlays - floating menus


Spatial UI
UI arranged in 3D space and anchored to the user or environment.
Examples: - world-locked panels - anchored windows in mixed reality

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Presence, usability and comfort
Good interaction design in XR should consider:

presence: does the interaction support the feeling of being there?
usability: can users understand what to do?
comfort: does the interaction reduce fatigue, confusion, and motion sickness?
accessibility: can different users complete tasks successfully?

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Framework for analysis: PACT







Element
Questions




People
Who are the users? What abilities, expectations, or limitations matter?


Activities
What are they trying to do?


Contexts
Where and when is the interaction taking place?


Technologies
What hardware, software, sensors, and constraints shape the experience?



PACT is a useful way to structure your case study.

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Example 1: Beat Saber



Aspect
Observation




Input
Two 6DOF controllers


Interaction
Direct embodied slashing


Feedback
Strong visual, audio, and haptic feedback


Locomotion
Stationary


Strengths
Intuitive, immediate, highly embodied


Weaknesses
Can be physically tiring, limited interaction range

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Example 2: Pokémon GO



Aspect
Observation




Input
Touchscreen, mobile camera, GPS


Interaction
Tap, swipe, movement through physical space


Feedback
Visual and audio


Locomotion
Real-world walking


Strengths
Blends physical and digital context


Weaknesses
Environmental constraints, limited depth of interaction

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Example 3: HoloLens 2 spatial interface







Aspect
Observation




Input
Hand tracking, gaze, voice


Interaction
Air tap, grab, spatial manipulation


Feedback
Visual anchoring, audio, gesture response


Strengths
Spatial workflow, mixed reality context


Weaknesses
Narrower field of view than ideal, interaction learning curve

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Evaluating XR experiences
Evaluation helps us understand:

what works well
where breakdowns occur
what should be improved
whether the design supports user goals

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Heuristic evaluation for XR
Useful adapted heuristics include:

visibility of system status
natural mappings between action and effect
user control and freedom
consistency of interaction patterns
prevention of accidental actions
clear affordances
reduced memory load
comfort and accessibility

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Quick user testing in XR
A small user test can still be valuable.
Recommended process:

Give the user a short task
Observe where they hesitate or fail
Ask what confused them
Note physical discomfort or awkward movement
Identify improvements

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Common interaction problems in XR

unclear affordances
inconsistent controls
poor feedback
overcomplicated gestures
uncomfortable locomotion
UI placed too close or too far away
excessive physical fatigue

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Linking this to your assignment
For Assessment 2, you will do three things:

Analyse an existing XR experience
Prototype one key interaction from that experience
Evaluate your prototype

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Assessment 2: what to analyse
Your analysis should consider:

interaction design
input and output systems
feedback
presence and immersion
strengths and weaknesses
comfort and accessibility
relevant HCI and XR design principles

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Assessment 2: what to prototype
Recreate one key interaction using Unity or Lens Studio.
Possible examples:

object grab and manipulation
ray-based menu selection
gaze interaction
gesture input
teleportation or navigation mechanic

Keep it focused. A simple, functional prototype is better than an over-ambitious broken one.

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Assessment 2: what to evaluate
You should discuss:

what works well in your prototype
what does not work as well as the original
what design compromises you made
what you would improve next

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
section: Suggested structure for the case study report
text:
Suggested structure for the case study report

Introduction to the chosen experience
Critical analysis of the interaction design
Description of the prototype
Evaluation and reflection
Conclusion

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
What strong submissions usually do

analyse rather than describe
connect theory to examples
focus on one interaction and do it well
identify clear strengths and limitations
use appropriate XR terminology accurately

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Common mistakes to avoid

choosing too many interactions
describing features without critique
building something unrelated to the analysis
ignoring comfort or usability
failing to reflect on limitations

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Week 6 lab activity
In the lab, you should:

choose your XR experience
identify one key interaction
begin your analysis notes
set up your Unity or Lens Studio prototype scene

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Suggested discussion prompt
Choose an XR application and answer:

what is the core interaction?
why does it work?
what assumptions does it make about the user?
how could it fail for a novice user?

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Key takeaway
A strong XR experience is not just technically impressive.
It combines:

appropriate input
clear feedback
comfort
usability
meaningful spatial design

title: Virtual, Augmented And Spatial Computing
text:
Next week

Environment design in VR, AR and spatial computing
We will move from interaction mechanics to space, layout, atmosphere, and behavioural design.

title: Assessment 2: XR Experience Analysis & Interaction Prototype
text:
In this assessment, you will critically analyse an existing immersive experience and recreate a key interaction from it as a working prototype.
This task combines analysis, design, and implementation, allowing you to demonstrate your understanding of XR systems and interaction design.

title: Assessment 2: XR Experience Analysis & Interaction Prototype
text:
In this assessment, you will critically analyse an existing immersive experience and recreate a key interaction from it as a working prototype.
This task combines analysis, design, and implementation, allowing you to demonstrate your understanding of XR systems and interaction design.

title: Assessment 2: XR Experience Analysis & Interaction Prototype
text:
Learning Outcomes

LO2: Critique and deconstruct XR experiences

LO3: Demonstrate practical competence with XR systems

LO4: Apply HCI principles in immersive environments

title: Assessment 2: XR Experience Analysis & Interaction Prototype
text:
Task

Part 1 — Experience Analysis
Select an XR experience (VR, AR, or spatial computing).
Analyse: - Interaction design - Presence and immersion - Spatial design - Strengths and weaknesses - Comfort and usability
Support with: - Screenshots or diagrams - References to lecture concepts



Part 2 — Interaction Prototype
Recreate one key interaction using Unity or Lens Studio.
Examples: - Object manipulation - Gesture interaction - UI selection (ray, gaze) - Navigation system
Your prototype must: - Be interactive and functional - Demonstrate understanding of XR input/output



Part 3 — Evaluation
Evaluate your prototype: - What works well? - What doesn’t? - How does it compare to the original? - What would you improve?

title: Assessment 2: XR Experience Analysis & Interaction Prototype
text:
Submission
Submit:

Report (1500–2000 words)
Prototype build (Unity / Lens Studio)
Video demo (2–3 minutes)

text:
Tips

Focus on interaction design
Link your work to module concepts
Keep your prototype simple but functional
